bibliography.abstract: Abstract Urban heritage scholars have often criticized simulacra as ‘bad’ copies that degrade the ‘good’ model of the past through commercialization and gentrification. This article challenges such Platonic dichotomies of good/bad and model/copy, arguing that the binary of good heritage and bad simulacra is flawed because heritage is itself actualized only as simulacra —a process of becoming that generates new trajectories and connections to all possible pasts. Drawing on an ethnographic study of Seochon Hanok Village in Seoul, South Korea, the article explores how various urban actors differently imagine and perform heritage in and through ongoing conflicts and negotiations to authenticate their divergent and coexisting simulacra of the past. Consequently, the article argues that a more inclusive approach to urban heritage emerges not by protecting a supposedly good heritage, but by embracing the ceaseless becomings and differences that revive all possible pasts as simulacra.

bibliography.title: ALL POSSIBLE PASTS: Heritage, Simulacra, and Gentrification in Seoul

publication_status.journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research

en.caveats: The findings are based on a qualitative, ethnographic investigation of a single historic neighborhood in Seoul, which may limit direct generalizability to cities with different heritage governance frameworks.
en.what: This paper presents an ethnographic study of Seochon Hanok Village in Seoul, South Korea, examining how diverse urban actors negotiate, conflict over, and perform different versions of the past. It challenges the traditional academic dichotomy that views heritage as an authentic model and commercialized simulacra as degraded copies, demonstrating instead how heritage is actively constructed through these competing representations.
en.why: It reframes urban heritage preservation by showing that heritage is not a static asset to be protected from commercialization, but an ongoing process of creation where multiple, coexisting versions of the past are continually produced and authenticated.
